chapter: After the road: New York, the profession and advice
title: The Thad Jones-Mel Lewis band
summary: Thad Jones asked him back to tenor trombone to play plunger; Jackson praises Jones's humorous writing and conducting but dislikes touring.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: to say, we'll be glad to hear it. All right. I'm sorry that I didn't get through the Thad Jones-Mel Lewis band.
Well, just talk about it. We've got time.
Well, you know, --
Because you've played in this great band. How did you get in the band? Who asked you? Let's get into it.

Well, you know, Thad and I was in Basie's band together. And Thad, he didn't really know -- because I started playing bass trombone, you see, and by me playing bass trombone everybody thought that I had quit playing tenor altogether, you see. So Thad said, 'I want you in my band.' Benny Powell was leaving the band, you know, because he was with Merv Griffin and they're going to California. The show moved to California, the Merv Griffin show.
Right.

So I said sure and he said, 'We've got a bass trombone here.' He said, 'Why don't you go back and play your tenor because people would like to hear you play the plunger again.' So I said, 'Well, okay.' So I went back and started to playing the tenor again and he started to writing some things for me to play with the plunger. And the
Oh, yeah.
And that is a very interesting orchestra. I think Thad Jones has got the greatest, one of the greatest bands today --
I believe it.
-- because it is modern. Yet and still, it is not overdone. It is sensible. And he is a great writer. He writes beautiful. He can write very pretty, and he has a lot of humor in his writing.
That's right.
You can listen to him, to his music, it will make you laugh, you know.
Right.
You can listen to it, it will make you cry. And you can listen to it and relax. And I think he's the greatest arranger today. I still think Thad Jones is the greatest arranger today.
I agree with you. I'm sure he's one of the greatest.
Yes.
He's so creative. How about his conducting which I always admired?
Oh, that is a picture, to watch him conduct, to bring different things out of the band that he
wants brought out. And you have to watch him, you know, because he'll cut you out any time. If he figures somebody's playing a good solo, he'll cut you out.
Yeah, he's quite a unique --
Yes. And then he'll put that hand up and do this. That means you come in; at the end of the next chorus you come back in. You know, when he puts that fist up there.
Sure.
But he can conduct. I love to watch him. I love to watch him conduct. He's a picture.
No question.
And he loves his music, you see. He loves his music very much, and can play.
Oh, he can play beautifully.
Can play. He has a style to me all his own.
Yeah.
Beautiful, beautiful. A beautiful trumpet player and to me he's a beautiful man, too.
The only reason that I'm not playing with that band right now, Milt, is because, like I told you before, I don't like traveling.
Uh-huh.
But anytime I can go sit in that band,
Uh-huh.
-- you see?
Thank you, Butter.
